principles.text: Your revenue ceiling is new MRR per month divided by monthly cancellation rate; halve churn and the ceiling doubles.
Position around more of what the buyer values, like growth, not cost savings; the same product can then command 8-10x the price.
Build strategy on deliberate weaknesses that enable strengths; competitors copy strengths but never weaknesses.
Before building, find ten people who say they'll pay, and interview against written hypotheses until you stop being surprised.
Hire people better than you at every role, or the organization just gets larger instead of better.

sampleQA.question: Our SaaS growth has stalled. Where do I start?

answer.text: Compute Max MRR: new MRR per month divided by monthly cancellation rate. That is where you plateau if nothing changes.
Fix churn first. Ask 'what made you cancel?', not 'why', and don't accept 'too expensive' as the real reason. Start with onboarding, since most cancellations happen early.
Then look at price. Your prices are almost certainly not optimal, and raising them often leaves signups flat.
Check which channels are saturated. Each campaign ramps, plateaus and declines, so pushing harder on a sagging channel won't restart growth.

sampleQA.question: How should a bootstrapped SaaS price?

answer.text: Charge $30-$80/mo, not $10. At $10 you can't afford marketing and need thousands of customers to be sustainable.
Raise prices far more than feels safe, and keep doubling until signups actually drop.
Offer an annual plan at 12x the current monthly price, then raise monthly about 20%. The year of cash arrives before the ad bill is due.
Consider replacing a free trial with a 60-day money-back guarantee; at WP Engine signups and customer counts went up.

sampleQA.question: Should we target a narrow niche or a broad market?

answer.text: Narrow. Write everything for one ideal customer; buyers with similar trade-off preferences make the effective market 10-100x larger.
Define that market by shared needs and use-cases, not company size or geography.
Ignore out-of-scope feature requests, and turn down big non-ICP customers even when the revenue is tempting.
